prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, made with the ATLAS and CMS detectors at the Large Hadron Collider

statement.case_for: The 2012 observation of the Higgs boson by two independently designed and built general-purpose LHC detectors is the one major experimental milestone in the Standard Model that the 2013 prize, which honoured the theory, left unrecognised. Four of eight members placed it first, but I rest the case on the science rather than on the tally: a new fundamental scalar was seen in several decay channels by two collaborations, and a decade of Run 1 to Run 3 data has fixed its mass, spin-parity and couplings at a level consistent with the Standard Model. The detector conception, construction and analysis effort is an instrumentation achievement of the first rank, and as an experimentalist I judge that the discovery has been mature for years. A single-part prize also gives the cleanest citation. I have moved my proposed names modestly after reading the other ballots: with Gianotti credited by seven of eight members and Jenni by five, I now put one founding ATLAS leader beside the ATLAS spokesperson at the time of the announcement and keep one CMS founder, so both experiments are represented. Virdee and Della Negra are close to interchangeable on the supplied evidence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The discovery belongs to two collaborations of thousands, the statutes allow at most three laureates, and any trio drawn from four credited leaders (Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) honours leadership and conception rather than a verifiable accounting of who made the decisive analysis contributions. Excluding one of two founding CMS or ATLAS figures will look arbitrary, and the committee may be unwilling to set a precedent of crediting collaboration leaders. A second concern is that the full Higgs-sector programme is still evolving, so some may argue for waiting. I think that concern is weaker than the attribution problem, because the discovery itself is secure and will not be revised.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery first as an empirical milestone not yet recognised and proposes Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee, accepting that Della Negra is a strong alternative and that the choice is open to dispute. He places IceCube fourth, with source identification still developing.
responses.response: I agree with the reasoning and have moved toward his trio, since it covers both experiments and the names with the widest support across the ballots. I do not think the Della Negra question can be settled from the supplied text, and I would not claim Virdee over Della Negra on merit. Where I differ is on IceCube: I ranked it second, but his point that the astrophysical sources are largely unidentified is fair, and I now treat it as an alternative rather than something ready to pair with the Higgs discovery.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first. He argues the concept is clear, the realisation decisive and the impact on precision measurement lasting, and that the 2005 frequency-comb prize makes this a timely continuation. He discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I respect the case. B013 is the most broadly supported entry across the committee, with all eight members ranking it and seven placing it in their top three, and I rank it third myself. I disagree about priority. Optical clocks are a refinement of a measurement tradition the Academy has recognised in 2005 and 2012, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, whereas the Higgs discovery has no earlier experimental recognition. His disclosure of a possible perceived tie to Hall's group is appropriate, and it affects how heavily the committee should weigh his advocacy rather than the science. I keep B013 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Johansson also ranks the Higgs discovery first and proposes Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, two ATLAS founders and one CMS founder, saying that the omission of Virdee and the balance between experiments are contestable. He notes recognition is arguably overdue.
responses.response: His trio is defensible and I take the omission of one CMS leader as seriously as he does. My concern is that two ATLAS and one CMS leader drops the CMS-side name with the strongest support on the other ballots. The committee will have to settle the split by an explicit principle, such as founder versus spokesperson at the time of discovery, and not by counting votes. I would accept his configuration if the committee prefers founding leaders to spokespersons, and I agree with him that the three-person cap is a statutory constraint and not evidence about who mattered most.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first on the grounds that it is a clear instrumental invention with decades of demonstrated downstream impact, and she notes the STEM corrector pioneers are missing from the credited names. She ranks the Higgs discovery fourth with attribution doubts.
responses.response: As someone who builds instruments I am sympathetic to the case, and she is right that the missing STEM-corrector credit is a real allocation problem. But B015 has only her support, and the unresolved TEM versus STEM credit makes a fair three-person citation harder than for the Higgs case, not easier. On her attribution worry about the Higgs, I agree that no three-person choice is uniquely fair, but I do not agree that this should push the discovery down: the difficulty is in the statute, not in the science.

uncertainties: Which of Della Negra and Virdee should accompany Gianotti and Jenni, and whether the committee prefers founders or announcement-time spokespersons, is not settled by the supplied evidence.
Whether the Academy would accept a prize that credits collaboration leaders for a discovery made by thousands.
Whether a two-part prize pairing the Higgs discovery with optical lattice clocks would be preferable to a single-part prize; the three-person cap makes this hard to credit fairly.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001: my doctorate was in experimental particle physics through Birmingham and CERN, but my documented collaborations are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, and the profile does not identify ATLAS, CMS or any credited name as a connection. I note field proximity, not a documented tie, for the astroparticle and gamma-ray entries (B059 IceCube, B033 H.E.S.S.), and would treat my enthusiasm there with caution.
